title: "I was sure I was going to die" - Jornet talks near-death experiences and the 2 survival skills he swears by
excerpt: The ultrarunning GOAT admits he’s made some bad decisions while running, but the thought of others dealing with the consequences of his death made him question some of the risks he now takes
content:
If you’re a fan of the Spanish ultrarunning legend, Kilian Jornet (and it’s fair to label him a legend), you’ll have seen plenty of his stomach-lurching videos of his runs along precarious ridgelines surrounded by unsettling drops into the abyss.

From these videos and his incredible running performances over the years – he's won UTMB four times, Sierre-Zinal 10 times, Zegama 11 times, Hardrock 100 five times and Western States, as well as summiting Everest twice, climbing 82 4,000m Alpine peaks in 19 days and most recently his States of Elevation project – we all know that the GOAT is as sure-footed as, well, a mountain goat, but even the best have their bad days and a bad day in the mountains can be life-threatening.

So all that elevation and climbing surely must have led to some hair-raising moments? That’s what Runner’s World Podcast hosts Ben Hobson and Rick Pearson asked Kilian when he appeared as a recent guest.

‘That day, I was sure I was going to die,’ Kilian said. ‘I was saying, “If I survive today, that will be a surprise.”’

The incident he was referring to took place during his project in the Alps in 2024. ‘I've taken some stupid decisions in the past,’ he said. ‘But I think I've been pretty good on assessing what my capacities are.’

This near-death experience occurred during the crossing between two mountains, and it made him question everything

‘It was a moment where I was a bit sad with myself,’ he says. ‘I was very aware that I was taking a risk that I thought was really unacceptable.’

This was the point that he was certain he would die. ‘I don’t know why I decided to keep going. It was not about the project or anything. I just continued and was aware of the risk.’

He says that usually, it feels easy for him to turn around. ‘When I had the avalanche in Everest and many other times, 50% of the time I turn around and I'm okay with that. I'm not fighting the decision.

‘That’s probably what has changed with [having] kids… but it’s not like the change happened overnight.’ He says he’s not afraid of dying – rather it’s the consequences his death brings to others that he’s afraid of. ‘That’s something that I’ve been thinking much more about lately.’

He admits it’s not always black and white when it comes to decision-making under pressure, and it’s often easier to turn around at the start of a big project rather than towards the end. ‘When you are close to achieving it, you think, “Ah, it’s only 10 metres,” And then the perception of risk is much lower.’

How to reduce the risks when mountain running

Despite the odd misjudgement now and again, Kilian has run some of the hardest routes in the world, and survived, and that doesn't happen by chance. It takes serious planning. Here are the two things that he does to make sure he's as safe as possible.

'I will always think on the worst case scenario' – Jornet admits that when planning adventures, he looks at exploring beautiful places for the simple joy of doing it, but will also look at each day and plan for the worst, 'I think, "Okay, I'm going to climb that summit," then it's like, "Okay, what if this happens? What if it's a thunderstorm? What if I fall into a crevasse? What if all these bad things happen?"' Then he can plan accordingly.

'Do I have the capacities, technical knowledge and the gear to get out from that.' – Alongside the planning, Jornet relies heavily on his experience and mountain skills to help whenever he faces trouble. Most issues for amateur runners arise in the mountains when the situation they are in turns bad and they lack the skill and kit to get themselves out of trouble. 'For me, it's not really about the summit, it's about the journey to get there. It's more the experiences that you will have along the way. Having a goal, like saying, "I want to climb Matterhorn," or, "I want to climb Mont Blanc," or, "I want to climb, um, this summit," it's a good goal to have, but not to have as an end point – it's about how you get there and to learn being in the mountains.'
